design_detail: Self-described systematic review with narrative synthesis (no pooling, no appraisal of included studies) of published numeric estimates of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018: 124 estimates from 27 studies. Its aim was explicitly not to produce rates but to map how the choice of starting sample (all people with alcohol problems, untreated people, or people already in remission) and the definitions of an alcohol problem, of remission and of treatment shape the estimates, for use in treatment-service planning (p. 61). Because it maps without appraising, it is rated with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief requires, not with AMSTAR 2; it does have a systematic search and explicit selection, which the first checklist domain records.
can_establish: That published estimates of untreated remission from alcohol problems span 2.7% to 98.3% and that much of this spread follows from which denominator is used and how an alcohol problem, remission and treatment are defined, with worked within-study examples.
cannot_establish: How many people with alcohol problems remit without treatment (no pooled or appraised estimate, by design), whether treatment changes the chance of remission (no treated comparison is analysed), or how far the figures apply outside North America or to recent years (24 of 27 studies are North American and 24 were published before 2010, editors' count).

sample.recruitment: Medline, PsycINFO and EMBASE searched on 10 November 2016 by one author with an expert librarian; further searches through Google Scholar, reference harvesting, the CORK Bibliography and consultation within the team, and checks by two authors up to April 2018; limits: human studies, English language, published after 1975 (p. 61, Methods › 2.2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: published journal articles giving a numeric estimate of untreated remission from alcohol problems, with no restriction on definitions, measures or design (p. 62, Methods › 2.4). Removed at screening: alcohol not the main focus (528), not about reducing alcohol use (146), formal treatment only (472), biological (357), no original data (48). Excluded at eligibility: self-help only as an adjunct to treatment (263), no separation of treated from untreated remission (51; for example Vaillant, 2003), substance use disorders without alcohol-specific data (29), mechanisms of change (127), stability of remission (2), no quantitative estimate (53). Dissertations, books and book chapters excluded (Fig. 1; pp. 61–62).
sample.demographics: Participant characteristics are not reported in the article (the study details are in the Supplementary Material, not read). Studies published 1976 to 2018; 24 of 27 (89%) North American, the others from Germany, the Netherlands and Poland; 12 longitudinal; 20 (74%) convenience samples, 1 probability sample (Kelly et al., 2018) and 6 population-based representative samples from the US, Canada, Germany and the Netherlands (p. 63, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the longitudinal studies is not reported in the article.
sample.selection_effects: English-language journal articles only, mostly North American convenience samples, and a dated literature, as the authors note (pp. 61, 70). Several included papers draw on one source cohort (Timko et al., 1993: people who had had a single detox episode or had contacted an information and referral centre, without other treatment), which contributes estimates to all three methods (Tables 1–4 footnote b, pp. 64–67). Studies that did not separate treated from untreated remission, including some long natural-history cohorts, were excluded (p. 62).

exposure.measurement: 'Untreated' as each study defined treatment, from formal alcohol treatment only to a definition counting formal treatment, self-help groups, informal help (for example clergy, college recovery programmes, employee assistance) and medical care; 27% of estimates used that broadest definition (p. 69, Results › 3.2.3; Table 5 note 3, p. 68). Some studies counted treatment for other mental-health problems as treatment; in the Timko-based studies, people seen once for detox or at an information and referral centre counted as untreated (Table 5 note 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Rarely addressed in the included studies, as the authors note; whether people who remit from alcohol without treatment seek treatment for another drug is unknown (p. 71, Discussion › 4.3, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Remission as each study defined it: abstinence only (41% of estimates), abstinence or moderate drinking (27%), no diagnosis (9%), no consequences (4%), and combinations; most studies used a one-year window; others used windows from six months to five years, or several follow-ups (pp. 68–69; Tables 1–3, 5).

comparison.controls: Not applicable: a descriptive review of proportions. The three 'methods' differ in their denominator: all people with an alcohol problem (method 1), untreated people with an alcohol problem (method 2), and people already in remission (method 3) (p. 63, Results › 3.1.1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Severity, psychiatric comorbidity and other drug use were rarely reported by the included studies (p. 71).

outcomes.instruments: Each study's own definitions, tabulated by method: alcohol problem by diagnosis (39% of estimates), consequences (20%), assumed from service contact (19%), consumption (9%) or consumption and consequences (12%); remission and treatment definitions as above (Tables 1–5, pp. 64–68; p. 69).
outcomes.validity_norms: No assessment of methodological quality or bias, by design (p. 70, Discussion › 4.2). Estimates marked 'a' in Tables 1–4 were calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data; how is described only in the Supplementary Material, not read.
outcomes.operationalization: Untreated remission expressed three ways: the share of all people with an alcohol problem who remitted without treatment (method 1); the share of untreated people with an alcohol problem who remitted (method 2); the share of people in remission who had not been treated (method 3) (p. 63).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests; summaries are ranges, medians and unweighted means of estimates.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Who screened, judged eligibility and extracted data is not stated; one author ran the database search and two authors ran further searches and checks (p. 61).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling (the literature was judged too heterogeneous, p. 62). All 124 estimates ranged from 2.7% to 98.3% (p. 63). In the nine studies with estimates for all three methods (23 estimates each, Table 4): method 1 2.7% to 63.6% (median 12.4, mean 21.5); method 2 6.5% to 77.9% (median 38.9, mean 40.9); method 3 4.3% to 94.2% (median 43.9, mean 42.7) (pp. 63, 67–68). Editors' calculation: these summaries reproduce from Table 4 as printed; with Table 3's method-3 values for Timko et al. (2000), the method-3 minimum becomes 6.4% and the mean 44.0, the median unchanged.
analysis.covariates: None. Effects of definitions are shown narratively, mainly through within-study contrasts in which the same sample is counted under different definitions.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA guidelines were applied to the search (p. 61).
analysis.selective_reporting: Study details are only in the Supplementary Material. The narrative reads one key within-study contrast against its own table (Cunningham, 1999; see reporting issues). A preliminary comparison of longitudinal and cross-sectional designs is reported only as showing no meaningful difference, without data (p. 70).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Published estimates of untreated remission from alcohol problems range from 2.7% to 98.3%. Estimates that start from people already in remission (method 3, the commonest kind) run highest; those that start from everyone with an alcohol problem (method 1) run lowest, with a median of 12.4% in the nine studies that allow all three methods. Broader remission definitions raise estimates under every method; narrower treatment definitions raise methods 1 and 3; stricter problem definitions can lower or raise estimates depending on method and remission definition.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract opens by stating that untreated remission from alcohol problems is common (p. 60), a premise the review does not quantify: the method that answers 'how many people with an alcohol problem remit without treatment' (method 1) gives mostly low figures over mostly one-year windows (editors' calculation from Table 1: median of the 37 method-1 estimates 14.8%, 28 of them below 30%). The text and discussion state that method-1 estimates are robust to the definition of an alcohol problem (pp. 69–70), which Table 1 contradicts for the one study that varied that definition (Cunningham, 1999: 6.7% rising to 25.9%). The suggestion that the findings apply across countries with established treatment systems rests on two population studies said not to deviate from the rest, without analysis (p. 71). Against this, the authors are explicit that the review was not designed to yield rates and did no quality appraisal (pp. 61, 70), and their main conclusion, that planners must choose the denominator and definitions to match the question and that remitted-sample estimates do not suit planning (pp. 70–71), follows from the tables.

timeline.event: Sobell, Cunningham & Sobell, two Canadian population surveys: 78% of people in remission had not been treated, the review's example of a 'remitted sample' figure (included study; pp. 61, 63; Table 3).

Sobell, Ellingstad & Sobell, methodological review of natural-recovery research, cited here for definitional variability and methodological weaknesses (p. 61; General list #24; not read for this card).

Dawson et al., NESARC 2001–2002: untreated-sample estimates of 12.4% with abstinence only and 32.6% with abstinence or moderate drinking (included study; p. 69; General list #22; not read for this card).

Fleury et al., meta-analysis of long-term remission in mostly treatment-recruited cohorts (35% to 54% after a mean 17 years); not cited by this review, and it classes the source cohort of Moos and Moos (2007) as a clinical sample.

replication.where_it_stands: A methodological map, not an estimate. It explains why figures such as 'most people recover without treatment' (a remitted-sample ratio) and much lower figures for the share of all people with an alcohol problem who remit untreated in a given year can both be correct. Any figure the encyclopedia quotes should come from a primary study, with its denominator, its definitions of problem, remission and treatment, and its time window.

funding.funder: The Drug Policy Modelling Program is funded by the Colonial Foundation Trust and located at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, which is funded by the Australian Government; the Centre for Social Research in Health is supported by a grant from the Australian Government Department of Health. Alison Ritter holds a National Health and Medical Research Council Fellowship (APP1136944), Kari Lancaster a UNSW Scientia Fellowship, and Richard Mellor a National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre PhD Scholarship. The funders had no role in design, analysis, write-up or the decision to submit (p. 71).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at UNSW Sydney (Drug Policy Modelling Program; Centre for Social Research in Health). The review serves the authors' work on treatment-planning models, and the introduction quotes their own planning paper (Ritter, Mellor et al., 2019) (p. 61); none of the 27 included studies is by the authors. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Population cohorts that assess alcohol use disorder with a standard interview at repeated, fixed intervals and record every form of help (formal treatment, mutual help, primary care, informal help), reporting all three ratios for the same people under stated definitions and windows; an individual-participant reanalysis of existing surveys named in the review (NESARC, the Netherlands Mental Health Survey and Incidence Study-2, the German TACOS) under common definitions is the achievable version.

domains.note: Three databases plus Google Scholar, reference harvesting and a specialist bibliography, with stated terms and limits and a PRISMA flow with counts and reasons (pp. 61–62); but English-language journal articles only, the database search was run by one author, and no duplicate screening or extraction is described.

No assessment of methodological quality or bias, by design (p. 70); estimates from convenience samples and from national surveys are tabulated side by side, and estimates calculated by the reviewers are explained only in the Supplementary Material.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 27 included studies is by the authors; only the motivation draws on their own planning work (p. 61).

Most conclusions are tied to tabulated contrasts, but the robustness of method-1 estimates to the problem definition is asserted against Table 1, the abstract's premise that untreated remission is common is not quantified, and cross-national applicability is suggested from two studies without analysis (pp. 60, 69–71).

domains.domain: Balance of populations and settings represented
domains.note: All numeric estimates were included whatever their size, so the range is not cherry-picked; but 24 of 27 studies are North American, 20 used convenience samples and 24 were published before 2010 (editors' count), so population-based and recent data from elsewhere are under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument fits a review that maps estimates without appraising them; under the round brief it is rated with the editors' narrative-review checklist rather than AMSTAR 2. (Had AMSTAR 2 been applied, confidence would be critically low: no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no appraisal of included studies.) The overall judgment follows the worst domain, the absence of any appraisal. The review may be cited for the spread of published estimates (2.7% to 98.3%), for the three denominators and why they give different answers, and for within-study examples of how definitions move the estimates (for example NESARC: 12.4% with abstinence only vs 32.6% with abstinence or moderate drinking). It should not be cited for a rate of untreated remission (the authors disclaim this), for the claim that method-1 estimates are robust to the problem definition, or for its unweighted medians and means as if they described a population.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 2,103 texts screened (2,081 from databases, 22 from other searches); 1,551 removed at screening and 525 at eligibility (263 self-help only as an adjunct to treatment, 51 no separation of treated from untreated remission, 29 no alcohol-specific data, 127 mechanisms of change, 2 stability of remission, 53 no quantitative estimate), leaving 27 studies. Databases searched on 10 November 2016; further searches and checks to April 2018; English, human studies, published after 1975.

No assessment of the methodological quality or bias of included studies was done, by design; synthesis was narrative because the literature was too heterogeneous for meta-analysis; study details are given only in the Supplementary Material.

27 studies published 1976–2018: 24 (89%) North American, 12 longitudinal, 20 (74%) convenience samples, 1 probability sample and 6 population-based representative samples (US, Canada, Germany, Netherlands). The 124 estimates of untreated remission ranged from 2.7% to 98.3%.

Three starting samples give three different quantities: method 1, the share of all people with an alcohol problem who remit without treatment (37 estimates from 11 studies, only 2 of which reported it directly, the rest calculated by the reviewers; for example 36.9% of people with non-comorbid and 42.6% with comorbid DSM-IV alcohol dependence in the German TACOS survey); method 2, the share of untreated people who remit (36 estimates from 16 studies); method 3, the share of people in remission who were never treated (51 estimates from 19 studies, the commonest approach; for example 78% in two Canadian population surveys, Sobell et al., 1996).

In the nine studies with estimates under all three methods (23 each): method 1 ranged 2.7% to 63.6% (median 12.4, mean 21.5), method 2 6.5% to 77.9% (median 38.9, mean 40.9) and method 3 4.3% to 94.2% (median 43.9, mean 42.7).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.2, 1st paragraph (starting p. 63, ending p. 68); Table 4 (p. 67)
key_findings.note: Unweighted summaries of estimates, several per study. Table 4's method-3 values for Timko et al. (2000) repeat its method-1 values; with Table 3's values the method-3 minimum is 6.4% and the mean 44.0 (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Studies drawing on one cohort of untreated people (seen after a single detox episode or at an information and referral centre; Timko et al., 1993) found 14.0% to 52.9% remitting (method 2). When Moos and Moos (2007) also required remission at the 16-year follow-up, the untreated-sample rate fell from 36.0% to 14.0%.

Definition of remission: 41% of estimates used abstinence only and 27% abstinence or moderate drinking; broader definitions raised estimates under all three methods (for example NESARC, Dawson et al., 2005, method 2: 12.4% with abstinence only vs 32.6% with abstinence or moderate drinking), and 'no diagnosis' definitions sat at the top of each method's range. Most studies used a one-year window; a six-month abstinence window gave 63% in one study (Tucker and Gladsjo, 1993).

Definition of an alcohol problem: diagnosis 39% of estimates, consequences 20%, assumed from service contact 19%, consumption 9%, consumption and consequences 12%. In the Netherlands (Tuithof et al., 2016), 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, but 40% of those with a moderate or severe disorder. In Cunningham (1999), the method-3 estimate with abstinence or moderation fell from 87.5% (one or more consequences) to 80.7% (two or more), 74.5% (three or more) and 53.7% (six or more).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (starting p. 68); Tables 3 and 5 (pp. 66, 68)
key_findings.note: For Cunningham (1999), the method-3 estimates with abstinence only rose from 46.5% to 80.5%, and the method-1 estimates rose from 6.7% to 25.9% (abstinence) and 13.8% to 31.8% (abstinence or moderation) (Tables 1 and 3).

key_findings.finding: Definition of treatment: 27% of estimates counted formal treatment, self-help groups, informal help and primary care as treatment. Narrower definitions raised method-1 and method-3 estimates: in the Dutch survey, counting only alcohol treatment gave 63.6% (method 1) and 94.2% (method 3), against 42.9% and 63.5% when general treatment for other mental-health problems also counted; method-2 estimates changed little.
key_findings.note: The text describes the narrower Dutch definition as formal alcohol treatment alone; Tables 1 and 3 label it formal plus medical alcohol treatment.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: remitted-sample estimates (method 3), the commonest in the literature, are not useful for treatment planning because they start from people no longer in need; method-1 estimates suit planning for the total number needing treatment in a year, method-2 estimates the number of additional places needed for people not in treatment; most estimates cover about a one-year window, and longer planning horizons need studies with repeated assessments.

Context cited by the authors: about 20% of people with alcohol use disorders receive treatment in Europe and in the US, and 22% in Australia (from Probst et al., 2015; Grant et al., 2015; Teesson et al., 2010).
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; cite the primary sources.

key_findings.finding: Further points from the discussion: in a preliminary analysis, longitudinal and cross-sectional studies did not differ meaningfully (no data shown); population estimates from Germany and the Netherlands did not deviate from the rest; other drug use and mental-health comorbidity were rarely addressed, and in TACOS untreated remission did not differ significantly between people with and without comorbidity (as cited).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that, in Cunningham (1999), varying the definition of an alcohol problem did not affect method-1 estimates, and the review concludes that method 1 is more robust to that definition (pp. 69–70); Table 1 shows the method-1 estimates rising from 6.7% to 25.9% (abstinence) and from 13.8% to 31.8% (abstinence or moderation) as the definition tightens from one to six or more consequences (p. 64).
reporting_issues.consequence: The robustness claim, one reason given for preferring method 1, is not supported by the only study that varied the problem definition within method 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites Cunningham (1999) as showing that stricter problem definitions lower method-3 estimates (87.5%, 80.7%, 74.5% and so on), which holds for abstinence or moderation; for abstinence alone, Table 3 shows the method-3 estimates rising from 46.5% to 80.5% (pp. 66, 69).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the effect of the problem definition depends on the remission definition; the general statement that stricter problem definitions lower method-2 and method-3 estimates rests partly on one half of this study's data.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 repeats Timko et al. (2000)'s method-1 values (4.3%, 11.2%, 7.3%, 16.1%) in the method-3 column, while Table 3 gives that study's method-3 values as 8.0%, 20.9%, 12.5% and 27.6% (pp. 66–67).
reporting_issues.consequence: The method-3 range (from 4.3%) and mean (42.7) quoted in the text derive from the error; with Table 3's values the minimum is 6.4% and the mean 44.0 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 prints 15 (13.5%) for method-1 estimates defining remission as abstinence and 11 (18.9%) for the total of estimates using 'formal alcohol treatment excludes detox and I&R'; by the editors' arithmetic, 15 of 37 is 40.5% and 11 of 124 is 8.9%. Dawson et al. (2006)'s treatment definition is printed with 'AA' twice in Tables 1–4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the counts are consistent and the text's percentages are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The summaries (ranges, medians, means) treat each estimate as one unit although studies contribute between 1 and 12 estimates drawn from the same participants (Cunningham, 1999 alone gives 12 of the 37 method-1 estimates), and no weighting by sample size is used (pp. 63, 68).
reporting_issues.consequence: The medians and means describe the set of published estimates, not any population, and should not be quoted as rates.

reporting_issues.issue: Most method-1 estimates and many method-3 estimates are the reviewers' own calculations ('a' in Tables 1–4), described only in the Supplementary Material; the abstract reports 2,103 texts identified and Fig. 1 2,103 screened, although duplicates are said to have been removed, so the number of duplicates is not given (pp. 60, 62).
reporting_issues.consequence: The calculated estimates cannot be checked from the article; the Supplementary Material (at the article's DOI) is needed.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), pp. 60–72 (all pages; Tables 1–4, printed sideways on pp. 64–67, rotated and read at 220 dpi, Table 5 and Fig. 1 checked on rendered pages; every number on the card checked on the rendered pages). The online Supplementary Material (study details and the reviewers' calculations) was not among the files and was not read.
